   > “capillary: smallest of blood vessels where physical exchange occurs between the blood and tissue cells surrounded by interstitial fluid” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
4. These capillaries wrap around alveoli, tiny air sacs where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged. *(defines “alveoli”)*
   > “The pulmonary capillaries surround lung structures known as alveoli that are the sites of oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
   > “The bronchi branch into smaller and smaller passageways until they terminate in tiny air sacs called alveoli.” ([SEER Training Modules: Bronchi, Bronchial Tree, & Lungs](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/respiratory/passages/bronchi.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))

#### Pulmonary trunk: Plain (drafted; grade 8.7; `content/FMA_8612/tier1.md`)

1. The pulmonary trunk carries blood low in oxygen toward the lungs.
   > “The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary trunk, which leads toward the lungs and bifurcates into the left and right pulmonary arteries.” ([19.1 Heart Anatomy](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-1-heart-anatomy), CC BY 4.0)
2. The pulmonary trunk is the only vessel leaving the right ventricle, the heart's lower right pumping chamber. *(defines “right ventricle”)*
   > “The single vessel exiting the right ventricle is the pulmonary trunk.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
   > “the right ventricle is the major pumping chamber on the lower right side of the heart” ([Chapter 19 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: The Heart)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
3. A valve at the base of the pulmonary trunk keeps blood from flowing back into the right ventricle.
   > “At the base of the pulmonary trunk is the pulmonary semilunar valve, which prevents backflow of blood into the right ventricle during ventricular diastole.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
4. At the top of the heart, the pulmonary trunk splits into two pulmonary arteries, one for each lung. *(defines “pulmonary arteries”)*
   > “As the pulmonary trunk reaches the superior surface of the heart, it curves posteriorly and rapidly bifurcates (divides) into two branches, a left and a right pulmonary artery.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
   > “pulmonary arteries: left and right branches of the pulmonary trunk that carry deoxygenated blood from the heart to each of the lungs” ([Chapter 19 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: The Heart)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)

#### Radial artery: Plain (drafted; grade 7.8; `content/FMA_22730/tier1.md`; also Right radial artery, Left radial artery)

1. Each radial artery supplies blood to the forearm and wrist.
   > “radial artery: formed at the bifurcation of the brachial artery; parallels the radius; gives off smaller branches until it reaches the carpal region where it fuses with the ulnar artery to form the superficial and deep palmar arches; supplies blood to the lower arm and carpal region” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
2. Below the elbow, this artery branches off the brachial artery, the artery of the upper arm. *(defines “brachial artery”)*
   > “Branch of the brachial artery beginning below the elbow and extending down the forearm around the wrist and into the palm.” ([UBERON:0001404 radial artery](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/UBERON_0001404), CC BY 3.0)
   > “the majority of the vessel continues into the upper arm, or brachium, and becomes the brachial artery” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
3. The radial artery runs beside the radius, the forearm bone that gives this artery its name. *(defines “radius”)*
   > “The radial artery and ulnar artery parallel their namesake bones, giving off smaller branches until they reach the wrist, or carpal region.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
   > “radius: bone located on the lateral side of the forearm” ([Chapter 8 Key Terms (The Appendicular Skeleton)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/8-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
4. You can feel the pulse, an artery's stretch and recoil, at the radial artery in the wrist. *(defines “pulse”)*
   > “Pulse can be palpated manually by placing the tips of the fingers across an artery that runs close to the body surface and pressing lightly. While this procedure is normally performed using the radial artery in the wrist” ([20.2 Blood Flow, Blood Pressure, and Resistance](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-2-blood-flow-blood-pressure-and-resistance), CC BY 4.0)
   > “pulse: alternating expansion and recoil of an artery as blood moves through the vessel; an indicator of heart rate” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)

#### Renal artery: Plain (drafted; grade 8; `content/FMA_14751/tier1.md`; also Right renal artery, Left renal artery)

1. Each renal artery carries blood to a kidney, an organ that filters the blood. *(defines “kidney”)*
   > “Renal arteries branch repeatedly to supply blood to the kidneys.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
   > “The kidneys are the organs that filter the blood, remove the wastes, and excrete the wastes in the urine.” ([SEER Training Modules: Kidneys](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/urinary/components/kidney.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
2. The right and left renal arteries branch off the aorta, the largest artery in the body. *(defines “aorta”)*
   > “Either of two arteries (right or left) that arise from the aorta to supply the kidneys.” ([NCIT:C12778 Renal Artery](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/NCIT_C12778), CC BY 4.0)
   > “aorta: largest artery in the body” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
3. The right renal artery is longer than the left, because the aorta lies to the left of the spine.
   > “The right renal artery is longer than the left since the aorta lies to the left of the vertebral column and the vessel must travel a greater distance to reach its target.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
4. Each renal artery enters its kidney at the hilum, the curved-in part of the kidney's bean shape. *(defines “hilum”)*
   > “The ureter and renal vein leave the kidney, and the renal artery enters the kidney at the hilum.” ([SEER Training Modules: Kidneys](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/urinary/components/kidney.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
   > “The hilum is the concave part of the bean-shape where blood vessels and nerves enter and exit the kidney” ([41.2 The Kidneys and Osmoregulatory Organs](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/41-2-the-kidneys-and-osmoregulatory-organs), CC BY 4.0)

#### Right gastric artery: Plain (drafted; grade 9.4; `content/FMA_14776/tier1.md`)

1. The right gastric artery supplies blood to the stomach.
   > “right gastric artery: branch of the common hepatic artery; supplies blood to the stomach” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
2. The right and left gastric arteries both supply the lesser curvature, the curved-in edge of the stomach. *(defines “lesser curvature”)*
   > “Either of two arteries (left gastric and right gastric) that supply blood to the stomach and lesser curvature.” ([NCIT:C32654 Gastric Artery](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/NCIT_C32654), CC BY 4.0)
   > “the concave medial border is the lesser curvature” ([23.4 The Stomach](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-4-the-stomach), CC BY 4.0)
3. The right gastric artery comes off the common hepatic artery, which also sends arteries to the liver and gall bladder. *(defines “common hepatic artery”)*
   > “the common hepatic artery, which in turn gives rise to the hepatic artery proper to supply blood to the liver, the right gastric artery to supply blood to the stomach, the cystic artery to supply blood to the gall bladder” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)

#### Splenic artery: Plain (drafted; grade 8.6; `content/FMA_14773/tier1.md`)

1. The splenic artery brings blood into the spleen, where the blood is filtered.
   > “Blood enters the spleen through the splenic artery, moves through the sinuses where it is filtered, then leaves through the splenic vein.” ([SEER Training Modules: Spleen](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/lymphatic/components/spleen.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
2. The splenic artery's four main branches supply the spleen, the stomach and the pancreas, a gland that releases digestive juices. *(defines “pancreas”)*
   > “An artery arising from the celiac trunk with four main branches that supply the spleen, stomach and pancreas.” ([NCIT:C33597 Splenic Artery](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/NCIT_C33597), CC BY 4.0)
   > “pancreas: gland that secretes digestive juices” ([Chapter 34 Key Terms (Animal Nutrition and the Digestive System)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/34-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
3. The splenic artery branches off the celiac trunk, a major artery that supplies blood to the digestive organs. *(defines “celiac trunk”)*
   > “splenic artery: branch of the celiac trunk; supplies blood to the spleen” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
   > “A major abdominal artery that arises from the abdominal aorta below the diaphragm. It supplies blood to the digestive organs. It has three major branches, left gastric artery, common hepatic artery, and splenic artery.” ([NCIT:C52846 Celiac Artery](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/NCIT_C52846), CC BY 4.0)

#### Subclavian artery: Plain (drafted; grade 9.1; `content/FMA_3951/tier1.md`; also Right subclavian artery, Left subclavian artery)

1. The subclavian arteries carry blood to the arms, chest, shoulders and back, and to the brain and spinal cord, which form the central nervous system. *(defines “central nervous system”)*
   > “Each subclavian artery supplies blood to the arms, chest, shoulders, back, and central nervous system.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
   > “central nervous system (CNS): anatomical division of the nervous system located within the cranial and vertebral cavities, namely the brain and spinal cord” ([Chapter 12 Key Terms (The Nervous System and Nervous Tissue)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/12-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
2. Each subclavian artery runs below the clavicle, or collarbone. *(defines “clavicle”)*
   > “An artery located below the clavicle that supplies blood to the head and the arms.” ([NCIT:C33643 Subclavian Artery](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/NCIT_C33643), CC BY 4.0)
   > “clavicle: collarbone” ([Chapter 8 Key Terms (The Appendicular Skeleton)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/8-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
3. The left subclavian artery branches directly off the arch of the aorta, the body's largest artery. *(defines “aorta”)*
   > “The brachiocephalic artery branches into the right subclavian artery and the right common carotid artery. The left subclavian and left common carotid arteries arise independently from the aortic arch” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
   > “aorta: largest artery in the body” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
4. But the right one branches off the brachiocephalic artery, the first branch of that arch. *(defines “brachiocephalic artery”)*
   > “subclavian artery: right subclavian arises from the brachiocephalic artery, whereas the left subclavian artery arises from the aortic arch” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
   > “brachiocephalic artery: single vessel located on the right side of the body; the first vessel branching from the aortic arch” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)

#### Superior mesenteric artery: Plain (drafted; grade 9.1; `content/FMA_14749/tier1.md`)

1. The superior mesenteric artery is the main blood supply of the small intestine, where most digestion and absorption take place. *(defines “small intestine”)*
   > “Parasympathetic nerve fibers from the vagus nerve and sympathetic nerve fibers from the thoracic splanchnic nerve provide extrinsic innervation to the small intestine. The superior mesenteric artery is its main arterial supply.” ([23.5 The Small and Large Intestines](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-5-the-small-and-large-intestines), CC BY 4.0)
   > “small intestine: section of the alimentary canal where most digestion and absorption occurs” ([Chapter 23 Key Terms (The Digestive System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
2. Branches of this artery also feed most of the large intestine, the last part of the digestive tract. *(defines “large intestine”)*
   > “The superior mesenteric artery arises approximately 2.5 cm after the celiac trunk and branches into several major vessels that supply blood to the small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, and ileum), the pancreas, and a majority of the large intestine.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
   > “large intestine: terminal portion of the alimentary canal” ([Chapter 23 Key Terms (The Digestive System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
3. The pancreas, an organ behind the stomach, gets blood from this artery too. *(defines “pancreas”)*
   > “superior mesenteric artery: branch of the abdominal aorta; supplies blood to the small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, and ileum), the pancreas, and a majority of the large intestine” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
   > “pancreas: organ with both exocrine and endocrine functions located posterior to the stomach that is important for digestion and the regulation of blood glucose” ([Chapter 17 Key Terms (The Endocrine System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/17-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
4. In the abdomen, this artery branches off the aorta, the body's largest artery. *(defines “aorta”)*
   > “superior mesenteric artery: branch of the abdominal aorta” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
   > “aorta: largest artery in the body” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)

#### Testicular artery: Plain (drafted; grade 9.5; `content/FMA_14758/tier1.md`; also Right testicular artery, Left testicular artery)

1. The testicular arteries carry blood to the testes, the male reproductive organs. *(defines “testes”)*
   > “Each gonadal artery supplies blood to the gonads, or reproductive organs, and is also described as either an ovarian artery or a testicular artery (internal spermatic), depending upon the sex of the individual.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
   > “The testes (singular = testis) are the male gonads—that is, the male reproductive organs.” ([27.1 Anatomy and Physiology of the Testicular Reproductive System](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/27-1-anatomy-and-physiology-of-the-testicular-reproductive-system), CC BY 4.0)
2. In the abdomen, each testicular artery branches off the aorta, the body's largest artery. *(defines “aorta”)*
   > “testicular artery: branch of the abdominal aorta” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
   > “aorta: largest artery in the body” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
3. Each testicular artery then leaves the body cavity to reach the testes.
   > “testicular artery: branch of the abdominal aorta; will ultimately travel outside the body cavity to the testes and form one component of the spermatic cord” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
4. On the way, each artery forms part of the spermatic cord, a bundle of nerves and blood vessels. *(defines “spermatic cord”)*
   > “It is considerably shorter than a testicular artery, which ultimately travels outside the body cavity to the testes, forming one component of the spermatic cord.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
   > “spermatic cord: bundle of nerves and blood vessels that supplies the testes; contains ductus deferens” ([Chapter 27 Key Terms (The Reproductive System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/27-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)

#### Thyrocervical artery: Plain (drafted; grade 8.4; `content/FMA_70346/tier1.md`; also Right thyrocervical artery, Left thyrocervical artery)

1. Each thyrocervical artery carries blood to the thyroid gland, an organ in the neck just below the voice box. *(defines “thyroid gland”)*
   > “The subclavian artery also gives rise to the thyrocervical artery that provides blood to the thyroid, the cervical region of the neck, and the upper back and shoulder.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
   > “The thyroid gland is a very vascular organ that is located in the neck. It consists of two lobes, one on each side of the trachea, just below the larynx or voice box.” ([SEER Training Modules: Thyroid & Parathyroid Glands](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/endocrine/glands/thyroid.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
2. This artery also feeds the neck, the upper back and the shoulder.
   > “The subclavian artery also gives rise to the thyrocervical artery that provides blood to the thyroid, the cervical region of the neck, and the upper back and shoulder.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
3. The artery is one of three major branches of the subclavian artery, an artery that feeds the arm and chest. *(defines “subclavian artery”)*
   > “Each subclavian artery supplies blood to the arms, chest, shoulders, back, and central nervous system. It then gives rise to three major branches: the internal thoracic artery, the vertebral artery, and the thyrocervical artery.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)

#### Ulnar artery: Plain (drafted; grade 9.1; `content/FMA_22796/tier1.md`; also Right ulnar artery, Left ulnar artery)

1. Each ulnar artery carries blood to the forearm, wrist and hand.
   > “A terminal branch of the brachial artery arising just below the elbow that runs along the ulna into the wrist with numerous branches supplying the forearm, wrist and hand.” ([NCIT:C12839 Ulnar Artery](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/NCIT_C12839), CC BY 4.0)
2. This artery begins where the brachial artery, the artery of the upper arm, splits into the radial and ulnar arteries. *(defines “brachial artery”)*
   > “As the brachial artery approaches the coronoid fossa, it bifurcates into the radial and ulnar arteries, which continue into the forearm, or antebrachium.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
   > “then becomes the brachial artery as it flows from the axillary region into the upper arm (or brachium)” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
3. The ulnar artery runs along the ulna, the forearm bone on the pinky-finger side. *(defines “ulna”)*
   > “ulnar artery: formed at the bifurcation of the brachial artery; parallels the ulna” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
   > “ulna: bone located on the medial aspect (pinky-finger side) of the forearm” ([Chapter 38 Key Terms (The Musculoskeletal System)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/38-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
4. At the wrist, the ulnar artery joins the radial artery to form the palmar arches, which supply blood to the hand. *(defines “palmar arches”)*
   > “The radial artery and ulnar artery parallel their namesake bones, giving off smaller branches until they reach the wrist, or carpal region. At this level, they fuse to form the superficial and deep palmar arches that supply blood to the hand” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
   > “palmar arches: superficial and deep arches formed from anastomoses of the radial and ulnar arteries; supply blood to the hand and digital arteries” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)

#### Vertebral artery: Plain (drafted; grade 9; `content/FMA_3956/tier1.md`; also Right vertebral artery, Left vertebral artery)

1. Each vertebral artery carries blood to the brain and spinal cord.
   > “The vertebral artery passes through the vertebral foramen in the cervical vertebrae and then through the foramen magnum into the cranial cavity to supply blood to the brain and spinal cord.” ([20.5 Circulatory Pathways](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-5-circulatory-pathways), CC BY 4.0)
2. This artery runs up through openings in the cervical vertebrae, the bones of the spine in the neck. *(defines “cervical vertebrae”)*
   > “vertebral arteries: arteries that ascend along either side of the vertebral column through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae and enter the cranium through the foramen magnum” ([Chapter 13 Key Terms (Anatomy of the Nervous System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
   > “cervical vertebrae: seven vertebrae numbered as C1–C7 that are located in the neck region of the vertebral column” ([Chapter 7 Key Terms (Axial Skeleton)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/7-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
3. The vertebral artery enters the skull through the foramen magnum, a large opening that the spinal cord passes through. *(defines “foramen magnum”)*
   > “foramen magnum: large opening in the occipital bone of the skull through which the spinal cord emerges and the vertebral arteries enter the cranium” ([Chapter 7 Key Terms (Axial Skeleton)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/7-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
4. Both vertebral arteries then merge into the basilar artery, which feeds the brain stem, the part of the brain joined to the spinal cord. *(defines “brain stem”)*
   > “The two vertebral arteries then merge into the basilar artery, which gives rise to branches to the brain stem and cerebellum.” ([13.3 Circulation and the Central Nervous System](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/13-3-circulation-and-the-central-nervous-system), CC BY 4.0)
   > “brainstem: portion of the brain that connects with the spinal cord” ([Chapter 35 Key Terms (The Nervous System)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)

### Cardiac

#### Heart: Core (drafted; grade 12.9; `content/FMA_7088/tier2.md`)

1. The heart is a muscular pump whose force keeps blood circulating to every tissue in the body.
   > “The heart is a muscular pump that provides the force necessary to circulate the blood to all the tissues in the body.” ([SEER Training Modules: Heart](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cardiovascular/heart/), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
2. It sits in the mediastinum, the space between the lungs, where a tough membrane called the pericardium separates it from the other structures there. *(defines “mediastinum”)*
   > “Within the mediastinum, the heart is separated from the other mediastinal structures by a tough membrane known as the pericardium, or pericardial sac, and sits in its own space called the pericardial cavity.” ([19.1 Heart Anatomy](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-1-heart-anatomy), CC BY 4.0)
   > “The human heart is located within the thoracic cavity, medially between the lungs in the space known as the mediastinum.” ([19.1 Heart Anatomy](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-1-heart-anatomy), CC BY 4.0)
3. It is a four-chambered organ about the size and shape of a closed fist, with two-thirds of its mass to the left of the body's midline.
   > “The human heart is a four-chambered muscular organ, shaped and sized roughly like a man's closed fist with two-thirds of the mass to the left of midline.” ([SEER Training Modules: Structure of the Heart](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cardiovascular/heart/structure.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
4. Two of its chambers, the thin-walled atria, receive blood from the veins, and the other two, the thick-walled ventricles, pump blood forcefully out of the heart. *(defines “atria”)*
   > “The two atria are thin-walled chambers that receive blood from the veins. The two ventricles are thick-walled chambers that forcefully pump blood out of the heart.” ([SEER Training Modules: Structure of the Heart](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cardiovascular/heart/structure.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
5. Blood travels from the right atrium to the right ventricle, out to the lungs to pick up oxygen, back to the left atrium, and then to the left ventricle, which pumps it into the systemic circulation, the route to the rest of the body. *(defines “systemic circulation”)*
   > “Blood flows from the right atrium to the right ventricle, and then is pumped to the lungs to receive oxygen. From the lungs, the blood flows to the left atrium, then to the left ventricle. From there it is pumped to the systemic circulation.” ([SEER Training Modules: Structure of the Heart](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cardiovascular/heart/structure.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
   > “For pulmonary and systemic circulation, the heart has to pump blood to the lungs or the rest of the body, respectively.” ([40.3 Mammalian Heart and Blood Vessels](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/40-3-mammalian-heart-and-blood-vessels), CC BY 4.0)
6. Two kinds of valves keep blood flowing in the right direction: atrioventricular valves between the atria and ventricles, and semilunar valves at the bases of the large vessels that leave the ventricles. *(defines “atrioventricular valves”)*
   > “The heart has two types of valves that keep the blood flowing in the correct direction. The valves between the atria and ventricles are called atrioventricular valves (also called cuspid valves), while those at the bases of the large vessels leaving the ventricles are called semilunar valves.” ([SEER Training Modules: Structure of the Heart](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cardiovascular/heart/structure.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
7. In each heartbeat, the myocardium, the thick layer of cardiac muscle cells in the heart wall, contracts in a phase called systole and then relaxes in a phase called diastole. *(defines “myocardium”)*
   > “The cardiac cycle refers to the alternating contraction and relaxation of the myocardium in the walls of the heart chambers, coordinated by the conduction system, during one heartbeat. Systole is the contraction phase of the cardiac cycle, and diastole is the relaxation phase.” ([SEER Training Modules: Physiology of the Heart](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cardiovascular/heart/physiology.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
   > “myocardium: thickest layer of the heart composed of cardiac muscle cells” ([Chapter 19 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: The Heart)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
8. The sinoatrial (SA) node, near the wall of the right atrium, is the heart's built-in pacemaker and sets the basic rhythm of the heartbeat; electrical pulses arise there on their own and make both atria contract together. *(defines “sinoatrial (SA) node”)*
   > “The internal pacemaker starts at the sinoatrial (SA) node, which is located near the wall of the right atrium. Electrical charges spontaneously pulse from the SA node causing the two atria to contract in unison.” ([40.3 Mammalian Heart and Blood Vessels](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/40-3-mammalian-heart-and-blood-vessels), CC BY 4.0)
   > “Because it establishes the basic rhythm of the heartbeat, it is called the pacemaker of the heart.” ([SEER Training Modules: Physiology of the Heart](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cardiovascular/heart/physiology.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
9. Each pulse then reaches the atrioventricular (AV) node, between the right atrium and right ventricle, where it pauses so the atria can empty completely into the ventricles before the ventricles pump the blood out. *(defines “atrioventricular (AV) node”)*
   > “then the pulse reaches the atrioventricular node between the right atrium and right ventricle. A pause in the electric signal allows the atria to empty completely into the ventricles before the ventricles pump out the blood.” ([40.3 Mammalian Heart and Blood Vessels](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/40-3-mammalian-heart-and-blood-vessels), CC BY 4.0)
   > “atrioventricular (AV) node: clump of myocardial cells located in the inferior portion of the right atrium within the atrioventricular septum; receives the impulse from the SA node, pauses, and then transmits it into specialized conducting cells within the interventricular septum” ([Chapter 19 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: The Heart)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
10. The right and left coronary arteries supply the myocardium itself with blood. *(defines “coronary arteries”)*
   > “The right and left coronary arteries, branches of the ascending aorta, supply blood to the walls of the myocardium.” ([SEER Training Modules: Structure of the Heart](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cardiovascular/heart/structure.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))

### Cell types

#### Basophil: Core (drafted; grade 10.9; `content/CL_0000767/tier2.md`)

1. A basophil is a white blood cell that releases chemicals to stimulate inflammation, a basic immune response. *(defines “inflammation”)*
   > “A basophil is a leukocyte that, like a neutrophil, releases chemicals to stimulate the inflammatory response” ([42.1 Innate Immune Response](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/42-1-innate-immune-response), CC BY 4.0)
   > “inflammation: basic innate immune response characterized by heat, redness, pain, and swelling” ([Chapter 21 Key Terms (The Lymphatic and Immune System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/21-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
2. It is a granular leukocyte, a white blood cell with abundant granules inside it. *(defines “granular leukocyte”)*
   > “Granular leukocytes contain abundant granules within the cytoplasm. They include neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils” ([18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets), CC BY 4.0)
3. Its granules release histamine, which contributes to inflammation, and heparin, which opposes blood clotting.
   > “The granules of basophils release histamines, which contribute to inflammation, and heparin, which opposes blood clotting.” ([18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets), CC BY 4.0)
4. Basophils hold serotonin as well as histamine, and they release these chemicals when properly stimulated.
   > “Basophils contain vasoactive amines such as histamine and serotonin, which are released on appropriate stimulation.” ([CL:0000767 basophil](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/CL_0000767), CC BY 4.0)
5. They also produce other inflammatory chemicals that recruit more white blood cells.
   > “Eosinophils and basophils produce additional inflammatory mediators to recruit more leukocytes.” ([42.1 Innate Immune Response](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/42-1-innate-immune-response), CC BY 4.0)
6. Mast cells, immune cells that produce histamine, share the basophil's role of intensifying the inflammatory response, but the two cell types develop from different cell lines. *(defines “mast cells”)*
   > “In general, basophils intensify the inflammatory response. They share this trait with mast cells. In the past, mast cells were considered to be basophils that left the circulation. However, this appears not to be the case, as the two cell types develop from different lineages.” ([18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets), CC BY 4.0)
   > “mast cell: leukocyte that produces inflammatory molecules, such as histamine, in response to large pathogens and allergens” ([Chapter 42 Key Terms (The Immune System)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/42-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
7. Basophils are the least common white blood cells, typically less than one percent of the total, and measure 8–10 µm in diameter.
   > “Basophils are the least common leukocytes, typically comprising less than one percent of the total leukocyte count. They are slightly smaller than neutrophils and eosinophils at 8–10 µm in diameter.” ([18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets), CC BY 4.0)
8. Their large granules stain best with basic, or alkaline, stains and turn dark blue; they are so common that they can make the two-lobed nucleus hard to see.
   > “The granules of basophils stain best with basic (alkaline) stains. Basophils contain large granules that pick up a dark blue stain and are so common they may make it difficult to see the two-lobed nucleus.” ([18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets), CC BY 4.0)
9. Basophils arise from myeloid stem cells, which also give rise to red blood cells and some other white blood cells. *(defines “myeloid stem cells”)*
   > “Myeloid stem cells give rise to all the other formed elements, including the erythrocytes; megakaryocytes that produce platelets; and a myeloblast lineage that gives rise to monocytes and three forms of granular leukocytes: neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils.” ([18.2 Production of the Formed Elements](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-2-production-of-the-formed-elements), CC BY 4.0)

#### Cardiac muscle cell: Plain (drafted; grade 8.9; `content/CL_0000746/tier1.md`)

1. Cardiac muscle cells, also called cardiomyocytes, do the heart's pumping and make up the heart muscle.
   > “The pumping of the heart is a function of the cardiac muscle cells, or cardiomyocytes, that make up the heart muscle.” ([40.3 Mammalian Heart and Blood Vessels](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/40-3-mammalian-heart-and-blood-vessels), CC BY 4.0)
2. They can contract in their own built-in rhythm, with no outside signal.
   > “A principal characteristic of cardiomyocytes is that they contract on their own intrinsic rhythms without any external stimulation.” ([4.4 Muscle Tissue and Motion](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-4-muscle-tissue-and-motion), CC BY 4.0)
3. Neighboring cells are joined by intercalated discs, junctions that help pass electrical signals from one cell to the next. *(defines “intercalated disc”)*
   > “This line is called an intercalated disc: it assists in passing electrical impulse efficiently from one cell to the next and maintains the strong connection between neighboring cardiac cells.” ([33.2 Animal Primary Tissues](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/33-2-animal-primary-tissues), CC BY 4.0)
   > “intercalated disc: physical junction between adjacent cardiac muscle cells” ([Chapter 19 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: The Heart)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
4. Because the cells are linked physically and electrically, the whole heart contracts as one unit.
   > “Cardiac muscle fibers each have one to two nuclei and are physically and electrically connected to each other so that the entire heart contracts as one unit (called a syncytium).” ([10.1 Overview of Muscle Tissues](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-1-overview-of-muscle-tissues), CC BY 4.0)

#### Cardiac muscle cell: Core (drafted; grade 10.3; `content/CL_0000746/tier2.md`)

1. Cardiac muscle cells, or cardiomyocytes, make up the heart muscle and carry out the heart's pumping.
   > “The pumping of the heart is a function of the cardiac muscle cells, or cardiomyocytes, that make up the heart muscle.” ([40.3 Mammalian Heart and Blood Vessels](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/40-3-mammalian-heart-and-blood-vessels), CC BY 4.0)
2. Together they form the myocardium, the middle layer and the bulk of the heart wall. *(defines “myocardium”)*
   > “myocardium: heart muscle cells that make up the middle layer and the bulk of the heart wall” ([Chapter 40 Key Terms (The Circulatory System)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/40-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
3. Under a microscope they look striated, or striped, and each typically has a single nucleus in its center. *(defines “striated”)*
   > “The cells of cardiac muscle, known as cardiomyocytes, also appear striated under the microscope. Unlike skeletal muscle fibers, cardiomyocytes are single cells typically with a single centrally located nucleus.” ([4.4 Muscle Tissue and Motion](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-4-muscle-tissue-and-motion), CC BY 4.0)
   > “The actin and myosin proteins are arranged very regularly in the cytoplasm of individual muscle cells (referred to as fibers) in both skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle, which creates a pattern, or stripes, called striations.” ([10.1 Overview of Muscle Tissues](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-1-overview-of-muscle-tissues), CC BY 4.0)
4. Their plentiful mitochondria, the cell parts that produce energy, power the heart's contractions. *(defines “mitochondria”)*
   > “Mitochondria are plentiful, providing energy for the contractions of the heart.” ([19.2 Cardiac Muscle and Electrical Activity](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-2-cardiac-muscle-and-electrical-activity), CC BY 4.0)
   > “mitochondrion: one of the cellular organelles bound by a double lipid bilayer that function primarily in the production of cellular energy (ATP)” ([Chapter 3 Key Terms (The Cellular Level of Organization)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/3-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
5. The cells branch and join end to end at intercalated discs, the junctions between neighboring cardiac muscle cells. *(defines “intercalated disc”)*
   > “Cardiac muscle fibers cells also are extensively branched and are connected to one another at their ends by intercalated discs.” ([10.7 Cardiac Muscle Tissue](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-7-cardiac-muscle-tissue), CC BY 4.0)
   > “intercalated disc: physical junction between adjacent cardiac muscle cells” ([Chapter 19 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: The Heart)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
6. Gap junctions in the discs form channels between neighboring cells, so electrical impulses spread from cell to cell and the cells contract in a coordinated way. *(defines “gap junction”)*
   > “Gap junctions within the intercalated disks allow impulses to spread from one cardiac muscle cell to another, allowing sodium, potassium, and calcium ions to flow between adjacent cells, propagating the action potential, and ensuring coordinated contractions.” ([19.2 Cardiac Muscle and Electrical Activity](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-2-cardiac-muscle-and-electrical-activity), CC BY 4.0)
   > “A gap junction forms channels between adjacent cardiac muscle fibers” ([10.7 Cardiac Muscle Tissue](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-7-cardiac-muscle-tissue), CC BY 4.0)
7. The rest of each disc is made of desmosomes, structures that anchor the ends of the cells together so they do not pull apart as they contract. *(defines “desmosome”)*
   > “The remainder of the intercalated disc is composed of desmosomes. A desmosome is a cell structure that anchors the ends of cardiac muscle fibers together so the cells do not pull apart during the stress of individual fibers contracting” ([10.7 Cardiac Muscle Tissue](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/10-7-cardiac-muscle-tissue), CC BY 4.0)
8. Cardiomyocytes can also contract in their own rhythm without outside stimulation, an ability called autorhythmicity. *(defines “autorhythmicity”)*
   > “A principal characteristic of cardiomyocytes is that they contract on their own intrinsic rhythms without any external stimulation.” ([4.4 Muscle Tissue and Motion](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-4-muscle-tissue-and-motion), CC BY 4.0)
   > “autorhythmicity: ability of cardiac muscle to initiate its own electrical impulse that triggers the mechanical contraction that pumps blood at a fixed pace without nervous or endocrine control” ([Chapter 19 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: The Heart)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
9. Most cardiac muscle cells are myocardial contractile cells, which contract to propel blood. *(defines “myocardial contractile cells”)*
   > “myocardial contractile cells: bulk of the cardiac muscle cells in the atria and ventricles that conduct impulses and contract to propel blood” ([Chapter 19 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: The Heart)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
10. Myocardial conducting cells, the other major type, carry electrical impulses through the heart and trigger those contractions. *(defines “myocardial conducting cells”)*
   > “There are two major types of cardiac muscle cells: myocardial contractile cells and myocardial conducting cells.” ([19.2 Cardiac Muscle and Electrical Activity](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-2-cardiac-muscle-and-electrical-activity), CC BY 4.0)
   > “myocardial conducting cells: specialized cells that transmit electrical impulses throughout the heart and trigger contraction by the myocardial contractile cells” ([Chapter 19 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: The Heart)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/19-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)

#### Erythrocyte: Plain (drafted; grade 6.9; `content/CL_0000232/tier1.md`)

1. An erythrocyte, or red blood cell, carries oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues. *(defines “erythrocyte”)*
   > “The primary functions of erythrocytes are to pick up inhaled oxygen from the lungs and transport it to the body’s tissues, and to pick up some (about 24 percent) carbon dioxide waste at the tissues and transport it to the lungs for exhalation.” ([18.3 Erythrocytes](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes), CC BY 4.0)
   > “erythrocyte: (also, red blood cell) mature myeloid blood cell that is composed mostly of hemoglobin and functions primarily in the transportation of oxygen and carbon dioxide” ([Chapter 18 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
2. It also takes some carbon dioxide waste from the tissues back to the lungs.
   > “The primary functions of erythrocytes are to pick up inhaled oxygen from the lungs and transport it to the body’s tissues, and to pick up some (about 24 percent) carbon dioxide waste at the tissues and transport it to the lungs for exhalation.” ([18.3 Erythrocytes](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes), CC BY 4.0)
3. It is made in the bone marrow, the tissue inside bones, and circulates through the body. *(defines “bone marrow”)*
   > “Red blood cells, or erythrocytes (erythro- = “red”; -cyte = “cell”), are specialized cells that circulate through the body delivering oxygen to cells; they are formed from stem cells in the bone marrow.” ([40.2 Components of the Blood](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/40-2-components-of-the-blood), CC BY 4.0)
   > “bone marrow: tissue found inside bones; the site of all blood cell differentiation and maturation of B lymphocytes” ([Chapter 21 Key Terms (The Lymphatic and Immune System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/21-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
4. It is packed with hemoglobin, a compound that carries oxygen. *(defines “hemoglobin”)*
   > “The most abundant formed elements in blood, erythrocytes are red, biconcave disks packed with an oxygen-carrying compound called hemoglobin.” ([18.3 Erythrocytes](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes), CC BY 4.0)
   > “hemoglobin: oxygen-carrying compound in erythrocytes” ([Chapter 18 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)

#### Erythrocyte: Core (drafted; grade 10.7; `content/CL_0000232/tier2.md`)

1. An erythrocyte, or red blood cell, carries oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues and brings some carbon dioxide waste back to the lungs. *(defines “erythrocyte”)*
   > “The primary functions of erythrocytes are to pick up inhaled oxygen from the lungs and transport it to the body’s tissues, and to pick up some (about 24 percent) carbon dioxide waste at the tissues and transport it to the lungs for exhalation.” ([18.3 Erythrocytes](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes), CC BY 4.0)
   > “erythrocyte: (also, red blood cell) mature myeloid blood cell that is composed mostly of hemoglobin and functions primarily in the transportation of oxygen and carbon dioxide” ([Chapter 18 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
2. It forms in the bone marrow, the tissue inside bones, and then circulates through the body. *(defines “bone marrow”)*
   > “Red blood cells, or erythrocytes (erythro- = “red”; -cyte = “cell”), are specialized cells that circulate through the body delivering oxygen to cells; they are formed from stem cells in the bone marrow.” ([40.2 Components of the Blood](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/40-2-components-of-the-blood), CC BY 4.0)
   > “bone marrow: tissue found inside bones; the site of all blood cell differentiation and maturation of B lymphocytes” ([Chapter 21 Key Terms (The Lymphatic and Immune System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/21-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
3. As it matures in the red bone marrow, it pushes out its nucleus and most other organelles, the small working parts inside a cell. *(defines “organelles”)*
   > “As an erythrocyte matures in the red bone marrow, it extrudes its nucleus and most of its other organelles.” ([18.3 Erythrocytes](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes), CC BY 4.0)
   > “organelle: small structures that exist within cells and carry out cellular functions” ([Chapter 1 Key Terms (The Study of Life)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/1-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
4. Lacking most organelles leaves it more room inside for hemoglobin, an oxygen-carrying compound. *(defines “hemoglobin”)*
   > “Since they lack most organelles, there is more interior space for the presence of the hemoglobin molecules that, as you will see shortly, transport gases.” ([18.3 Erythrocytes](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes), CC BY 4.0)
   > “hemoglobin: oxygen-carrying compound in erythrocytes” ([Chapter 18 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
5. Each hemoglobin molecule holds four heme groups, iron-containing pigments that bind oxygen, so it can carry up to four oxygen molecules. *(defines “heme”)*
   > “Each hemoglobin molecule contains four iron-containing heme molecules, and because of this, one hemoglobin molecule is capable of carrying up to four molecules of oxygen.” ([22.5 Transport of Gases](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/22-5-transport-of-gases), CC BY 4.0)
   > “heme: red, iron-containing pigment to which oxygen binds in hemoglobin” ([Chapter 18 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
6. Because it has no mitochondria, the organelles whose main job is making cellular energy, it uses none of the oxygen it carries and can deliver it all to the tissues. *(defines “mitochondria”)*
   > “Lacking mitochondria, for example, they rely on anaerobic respiration. This means that they do not utilize any of the oxygen they are transporting, so they can deliver it all to the tissues.” ([18.3 Erythrocytes](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes), CC BY 4.0)
   > “mitochondrion: one of the cellular organelles bound by a double lipid bilayer that function primarily in the production of cellular energy (ATP)” ([Chapter 3 Key Terms (The Cellular Level of Organization)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/3-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
7. Its shape is a biconcave disk, which means it is plump around the edge and very thin in the center. *(defines “biconcave”)*
   > “Erythrocytes are biconcave disks; that is, they are plump at their periphery and very thin in the center” ([18.3 Erythrocytes](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes), CC BY 4.0)
8. This shape gives it more surface area for exchanging gases, relative to its volume, than a sphere of similar width would have.
   > “The biconcave shape also provides a greater surface area across which gas exchange can occur, relative to its volume; a sphere of a similar diameter would have a lower surface area-to-volume ratio.” ([18.3 Erythrocytes](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes), CC BY 4.0)
9. Structural proteins such as spectrin let it change shape to squeeze through capillaries, the smallest blood vessels. *(defines “capillaries”)*
   > “Erythrocytes do, however, contain some structural proteins that help the blood cells maintain their unique structure and enable them to change their shape to squeeze through capillaries. This includes the protein spectrin, a cytoskeletal protein element.” ([18.3 Erythrocytes](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes), CC BY 4.0)
   > “capillary: smallest of blood vessels where physical exchange occurs between the blood and tissue cells surrounded by interstitial fluid” ([Chapter 20 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/20-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
10. After up to 120 days in the blood, worn-out erythrocytes are removed by macrophages, large engulfing cells found mainly in the bone marrow, liver and spleen. *(defines “macrophages”)*
   > “Erythrocytes live up to 120 days in the circulation, after which the worn-out cells are removed by a type of myeloid phagocytic cell called a macrophage, located primarily within the bone marrow, liver, and spleen.” ([18.3 Erythrocytes](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-3-erythrocytes), CC BY 4.0)
   > “macrophage: large phagocytic cell that engulfs foreign particles and pathogens” ([Chapter 42 Key Terms (The Immune System)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/42-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)

#### Macrophage: Plain (drafted; grade 6.8; `content/CL_0000235/tier1.md`)

1. A macrophage is a large cell that engulfs foreign particles and pathogens, agents that can cause disease. *(defines “pathogens”)*
   > “macrophage: large phagocytic cell that engulfs foreign particles and pathogens” ([Chapter 42 Key Terms (The Immune System)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/42-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
   > “pathogen: agent with the ability to cause disease” ([Chapter 21 Key Terms (Viruses)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/21-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
2. It also cleans up dead and damaged cells in the body.
   > “Monocytes give rise to phagocytic macrophages that clean up dead and damaged cells in the body, whether they are foreign or from the host animal.” ([33.2 Animal Primary Tissues](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/33-2-animal-primary-tissues), CC BY 4.0)
3. Macrophages live in many tissues of the body; some roam freely, while others stay fixed in place.
   > “Macrophages exist in many tissues of the body, either freely roaming through connective tissues or fixed to reticular fibers within specific tissues such as lymph nodes.” ([21.2 Barrier Defenses and the Innate Immune Response](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/21-2-barrier-defenses-and-the-innate-immune-response), CC BY 4.0)
4. They are monocytes, a type of white blood cell, that have left the bloodstream. *(defines “monocytes”)*
   > “Macrophages are monocytes that have left the circulation and phagocytize debris, foreign pathogens, worn-out erythrocytes, and many other dead, worn out, or damaged cells.” ([18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets), CC BY 4.0)
   > “monocyte: type of white blood cell that circulates in the blood and lymph and differentiates into macrophages after it moves into infected tissue” ([Chapter 42 Key Terms (The Immune System)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/42-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)

#### Macrophage: Core (drafted; grade 12; `content/CL_0000235/tier2.md`)

1. A macrophage engulfs pathogens, which are agents that can cause disease, as well as debris, worn-out red blood cells and other dead or damaged cells. *(defines “pathogens”)*
   > “Macrophages are monocytes that have left the circulation and phagocytize debris, foreign pathogens, worn-out erythrocytes, and many other dead, worn out, or damaged cells.” ([18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets), CC BY 4.0)
   > “pathogen: agent with the ability to cause disease” ([Chapter 21 Key Terms (Viruses)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/21-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
2. Macrophages are monocytes, a type of white blood cell, that have left the bloodstream. *(defines “monocytes”)*
   > “Macrophages are monocytes that have left the circulation and phagocytize debris, foreign pathogens, worn-out erythrocytes, and many other dead, worn out, or damaged cells.” ([18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-4-leukocytes-and-platelets), CC BY 4.0)
   > “monocyte: type of white blood cell that circulates in the blood and lymph and differentiates into macrophages after it moves into infected tissue” ([Chapter 42 Key Terms (The Immune System)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/42-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
3. They live in many tissues of the body; some roam freely, while others stay fixed in place.
   > “Macrophages exist in many tissues of the body, either freely roaming through connective tissues or fixed to reticular fibers within specific tissues such as lymph nodes.” ([21.2 Barrier Defenses and the Innate Immune Response](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/21-2-barrier-defenses-and-the-innate-immune-response), CC BY 4.0)
4. Their names differ by tissue: Kupffer cells in the liver, alveolar macrophages in the lungs, and histiocytes in connective tissue, the tissue that holds the body's organs in place. *(defines “connective tissue”)*
   > “They are called different names, depending on the tissue: Kupffer cells in the liver, histiocytes in connective tissue, and alveolar macrophages in the lungs.” ([21.2 Barrier Defenses and the Innate Immune Response](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/21-2-barrier-defenses-and-the-innate-immune-response), CC BY 4.0)
   > “connective tissue: type of tissue that serves to hold in place, connect, and integrate the body’s organs and systems” ([Chapter 4 Key Terms (The Tissue Level of Organization)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
5. A macrophage has an irregular shape and moves through tissues using pseudopodia, extensions of the cell. *(defines “pseudopodia”)*
   > “A macrophage is an irregularly shaped phagocyte that is amoeboid in nature and is the most versatile of the phagocytes in the body. Macrophages move through tissues and squeeze through capillary walls using pseudopodia.” ([21.2 Barrier Defenses and the Innate Immune Response](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/21-2-barrier-defenses-and-the-innate-immune-response), CC BY 4.0)
   > “Still others form cytoplasmic extensions called pseudopodia anywhere on the cell, anchor the pseudopodia to a substrate, and pull themselves forward.” ([23.2 Characteristics of Protists](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/23-2-characteristics-of-protists), CC BY 4.0)
6. To engulf a pathogen, a macrophage uses phagocytosis: a section of its plasma membrane, the boundary between the cell and its surroundings, folds in around the pathogen. *(defines “plasma membrane”)*
   > “In a process that scientists call phagocytosis or endocytosis, a section of the macrophage's plasma membrane invaginates (folds in) and engulfs a pathogen.” ([4.4 The Endomembrane System and Proteins](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins), CC BY 4.0)
   > “plasma membrane: phospholipid bilayer with embedded (integral) or attached (peripheral) proteins, and separates the cell's internal content from its surrounding environment” ([Chapter 4 Key Terms (Cell Structure)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
7. The folded-in section pinches off with the pathogen inside and fuses with a lysosome, a part of the cell that contains digestive enzymes; these enzymes then destroy the pathogen. *(defines “lysosome”)*
   > “The invaginated section, with the pathogen inside, then pinches itself off from the plasma membrane and becomes a vesicle. The vesicle fuses with a lysosome. The lysosome’s hydrolytic enzymes then destroy the pathogen” ([4.4 The Endomembrane System and Proteins](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/4-4-the-endomembrane-system-and-proteins), CC BY 4.0)
   > “lysosome: membrane-bound cellular organelle originating from the Golgi apparatus and containing digestive enzymes” ([Chapter 3 Key Terms (The Cellular Level of Organization)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/3-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
8. When stimulated, macrophages release cytokines, small proteins that act as chemical messengers and recruit other immune cells to infected sites. *(defines “cytokines”)*
   > “When stimulated, macrophages release cytokines, small proteins that act as chemical messengers. Cytokines recruit other cells of the immune system to infected sites and stimulate their activities.” ([4.3 Connective Tissue Supports and Protects](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-3-connective-tissue-supports-and-protects), CC BY 4.0)
9. They also stimulate T cells, white blood cells that physically attack foreign or diseased cells, to release cytokines that strengthen phagocytosis. *(defines “T cells”)*
   > “Macrophages stimulate T cells to release cytokines that enhance phagocytosis.” ([21.3 The Adaptive Immune Response: T lymphocytes and Their Functional Types](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/21-3-the-adaptive-immune-response-t-lymphocytes-and-their-functional-types), CC BY 4.0)
   > “T lymphocytes: (also, T cells) lymphocytes that provide cellular-level immunity by physically attacking foreign or diseased cells” ([Chapter 18 Key Terms (The Cardiovascular System: Blood)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/18-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)

### Digestive

#### Appendix: Plain (drafted; grade 9.4; `content/FMA_14542/tier1.md`)

1. With its lymphoid tissue, clusters of immune cells, the appendix may help the immune system. *(defines “lymphoid tissue”)*
   > “Although the 7.6-cm (3-in) long appendix contains lymphoid tissue, suggesting an immunologic function, this organ is generally considered vestigial.” ([23.5 The Small and Large Intestines](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-5-the-small-and-large-intestines), CC BY 4.0)
   > “The lamina propria also serves an immune function by housing clusters of lymphocytes, making up the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT).” ([23.1 Overview of the Digestive System](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-1-overview-of-the-digestive-system), CC BY 4.0)
2. Still, most see the appendix as vestigial: a leftover from a distant ancestor, with no clear use. *(defines “vestigial”)*
   > “Although the 7.6-cm (3-in) long appendix contains lymphoid tissue, suggesting an immunologic function, this organ is generally considered vestigial.” ([23.5 The Small and Large Intestines](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-5-the-small-and-large-intestines), CC BY 4.0)
   > “vestigial structure: physical structure present in an organism but that has no apparent function and appears to be from a functional structure in a distant ancestor” ([Chapter 18 Key Terms (Evolution and the Origin of Species)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/18-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
3. However, one report suggests a possible use: storing gut bacteria to restock the gut after diarrheal illness.
   > “However, at least one recent report postulates a survival advantage conferred by the appendix: In diarrheal illness, the appendix may serve as a bacterial reservoir to repopulate the enteric bacteria for those surviving the initial phases of the illness.” ([23.5 The Small and Large Intestines](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-5-the-small-and-large-intestines), CC BY 4.0)
4. The appendix is a coiled tube attached to the cecum, the pouch where the large intestine begins. *(defines “cecum”)*
   > “appendix: (vermiform appendix) coiled tube attached to the cecum” ([Chapter 23 Key Terms (The Digestive System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
   > “cecum: pouch forming the beginning of the large intestine” ([Chapter 23 Key Terms (The Digestive System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)

#### Appendix: Core (drafted; grade 13.3; `content/FMA_14542/tier2.md`)

1. The appendix may play a part in immunity, because it contains lymphoid tissue, clusters of immune cells called lymphocytes. *(defines “lymphoid tissue”)*
   > “Although the 7.6-cm (3-in) long appendix contains lymphoid tissue, suggesting an immunologic function, this organ is generally considered vestigial.” ([23.5 The Small and Large Intestines](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-5-the-small-and-large-intestines), CC BY 4.0)
   > “The lamina propria also serves an immune function by housing clusters of lymphocytes, making up the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT).” ([23.1 Overview of the Digestive System](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-1-overview-of-the-digestive-system), CC BY 4.0)
2. In the inner layers of the appendix wall, this tissue takes part in sampling material from inside the gut, so the body can mount immune responses to potential pathogens, agents that can cause disease. *(defines “pathogens”)*
   > “M (or microfold) cells that sample material from the intestinal lumen and transport it to nearby follicles so that adaptive immune responses to potential pathogens can be mounted. A similar process occurs involving MALT in the mucosa and submucosa of the appendix.” ([21.1 Anatomy of the Lymphatic and Immune Systems](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/21-1-anatomy-of-the-lymphatic-and-immune-systems), CC BY 4.0)
   > “pathogen: agent with the ability to cause disease” ([Chapter 21 Key Terms (Viruses)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/21-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
3. Even so, the appendix is generally considered vestigial, a structure with no apparent function that seems left over from a working part in a distant ancestor. *(defines “vestigial”)*
   > “Although the 7.6-cm (3-in) long appendix contains lymphoid tissue, suggesting an immunologic function, this organ is generally considered vestigial.” ([23.5 The Small and Large Intestines](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-5-the-small-and-large-intestines), CC BY 4.0)
   > “vestigial structure: physical structure present in an organism but that has no apparent function and appears to be from a functional structure in a distant ancestor” ([Chapter 18 Key Terms (Evolution and the Origin of Species)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/18-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
4. The appendix is a winding tube about 7.6 cm (3 in) long, attached to the cecum, the pouch that forms the beginning of the large intestine. *(defines “cecum”)*
   > “The appendix (or vermiform appendix) is a winding tube that attaches to the cecum. Although the 7.6-cm (3-in) long appendix contains lymphoid tissue, suggesting an immunologic function, this organ is generally considered vestigial.” ([23.5 The Small and Large Intestines](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-5-the-small-and-large-intestines), CC BY 4.0)
   > “cecum: pouch forming the beginning of the large intestine” ([Chapter 23 Key Terms (The Digestive System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
5. Also called the vermiform, or worm-like, appendix, it sits at the ileocecal valve, where the ileum, the end of the small intestine, gives way to the large intestine. *(defines “ileum”)*
   > “The ileum ends and the large intestine begins at the ileocecal valve. The vermiform, “worm-like,” appendix is located at the ileocecal valve.” ([34.1 Digestive Systems](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/34-1-digestive-systems), CC BY 4.0)
   > “ileum: end of the small intestine between the jejunum and the large intestine” ([Chapter 23 Key Terms (The Digestive System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
6. A mesentery is a double sheet of membrane that suspends digestive organs; the appendix's own mesentery, the mesoappendix, tethers the appendix to the mesentery of the ileum. *(defines “mesentery”)*
   > “The mesoappendix, the mesentery of the appendix, tethers it to the mesentery of the ileum.” ([23.5 The Small and Large Intestines](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-5-the-small-and-large-intestines), CC BY 4.0)
   > “A fourth, the peritoneum, is the serous membrane in the abdominal cavity that covers abdominal organs and forms double sheets of mesenteries that suspend many of the digestive organs.” ([4.1 Types of Tissues](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-1-types-of-tissues), CC BY 4.0)
7. The appendix's twisted shape gives gut bacteria a sheltered place to gather and multiply.
   > “Moreover, its twisted anatomy provides a haven for the accumulation and multiplication of enteric bacteria.” ([23.5 The Small and Large Intestines](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-5-the-small-and-large-intestines), CC BY 4.0)

#### Esophagus: Plain (drafted; grade 8.2; `content/FMA_7131/tier1.md`)

1. The esophagus is a muscular tube that pushes swallowed food to the stomach.
   > “The esophagus is a tubular organ that connects the mouth to the stomach. The chewed and softened food passes through the esophagus after being swallowed. The smooth muscles of the esophagus undergo a series of wave like movements called peristalsis that push the food toward the stomach” ([34.1 Digestive Systems](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/34-1-digestive-systems), CC BY 4.0)
2. Waves of muscle contraction, called peristalsis, do the pushing. *(defines “peristalsis”)*
   > “Using peristalsis, or wave-like smooth muscle contractions, the muscles of the esophagus push the food towards the stomach.” ([34.1 Digestive Systems](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/34-1-digestive-systems), CC BY 4.0)
   > “peristalsis: wave-like movements of muscle tissue” ([Chapter 34 Key Terms (Animal Nutrition and the Digestive System)](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/34-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
3. The esophagus begins at the pharynx, or throat, and stays collapsed when you are not swallowing. *(defines “pharynx”)*
   > “The esophagus is a muscular tube that connects the pharynx to the stomach. It is approximately 25.4 cm (10 in) in length, located posterior to the trachea, and remains in a collapsed form when not engaged in swallowing.” ([23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-3-the-mouth-pharynx-and-esophagus), CC BY 4.0)
   > “pharynx: throat” ([Chapter 23 Key Terms (The Digestive System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
4. Along the way down, the esophagus lies behind the trachea, or windpipe. *(defines “trachea”)*
   > “As it descends, it is posterior to the trachea and anterior to the vertebral column.” ([SEER Training Modules: Pharynx & Esophagus](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/regions/pharynx.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
   > “The trachea, commonly called the windpipe, is the main airway to the lungs.” ([SEER Training Modules: Larynx & Trachea](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/respiratory/passages/larynx.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))

#### Esophagus: Core (drafted; grade 10.8; `content/FMA_7131/tier2.md`)

1. The esophagus is a muscular tube that carries swallowed food to the stomach.
   > “The esophagus is a tubular organ that connects the mouth to the stomach. The chewed and softened food passes through the esophagus after being swallowed. The smooth muscles of the esophagus undergo a series of wave like movements called peristalsis that push the food toward the stomach” ([34.1 Digestive Systems](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/34-1-digestive-systems), CC BY 4.0)
2. The esophagus begins at the pharynx, or throat, and stays collapsed when you are not swallowing. *(defines “pharynx”)*
   > “The esophagus is a muscular tube that connects the pharynx to the stomach. It is approximately 25.4 cm (10 in) in length, located posterior to the trachea, and remains in a collapsed form when not engaged in swallowing.” ([23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-3-the-mouth-pharynx-and-esophagus), CC BY 4.0)
   > “pharynx: throat” ([Chapter 23 Key Terms (The Digestive System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
3. Along the way down, the esophagus lies behind the trachea, or windpipe. *(defines “trachea”)*
   > “As it descends, it is posterior to the trachea and anterior to the vertebral column.” ([SEER Training Modules: Pharynx & Esophagus](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/regions/pharynx.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
   > “The trachea, commonly called the windpipe, is the main airway to the lungs.” ([SEER Training Modules: Larynx & Trachea](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/respiratory/passages/larynx.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
4. The esophagus then passes through an opening in the diaphragm, a dome-shaped breathing muscle, and empties into the stomach. *(defines “diaphragm”)*
   > “It passes through an opening in the diaphragm, called the esophageal hiatus, and then empties into the stomach.” ([SEER Training Modules: Pharynx & Esophagus](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/regions/pharynx.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
   > “the diaphragm, a dome-shaped respiratory muscle” ([SEER Training Modules: Anatomical Terminology](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/body/terminology.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
5. Peristalsis, waves of muscle contraction and relaxation, starts in the upper esophagus and pushes food toward the stomach. *(defines “peristalsis”)*
   > “Rhythmic waves of peristalsis, which begin in the upper esophagus, propel the bolus of food toward the stomach.” ([23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-3-the-mouth-pharynx-and-esophagus), CC BY 4.0)
   > “peristalsis: muscular contractions and relaxations that propel food through the GI tract” ([Chapter 23 Key Terms (The Digestive System)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
6. During peristalsis, a circular muscle layer squeezes the wall to force the food forward, while a lengthwise layer shortens the wall and widens it to receive the food.
   > “The circular muscle layer of the muscularis contracts, pinching the esophageal wall and forcing the bolus forward. At the same time, the longitudinal muscle layer of the muscularis also contracts, shortening this area and pushing out its walls to receive the bolus.” ([23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-3-the-mouth-pharynx-and-esophagus), CC BY 4.0)
7. Upper and lower sphincters, muscles that ring the tube and act as valves, control food moving into and out of the esophagus. *(defines “sphincter”)*
   > “Upper and lower esophageal sphincters control the movement of food into and out of the esophagus.” ([SEER Training Modules: Pharynx & Esophagus](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/regions/pharynx.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
   > “Recall that sphincters are muscles that surround tubes and serve as valves, closing the tube when the sphincters contract and opening it when they relax.” ([23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-3-the-mouth-pharynx-and-esophagus), CC BY 4.0)
8. The lower esophageal sphincter relaxes to let food into the stomach, then contracts to keep stomach acid from backing up into the esophagus.
   > “The lower esophageal sphincter relaxes to let food pass into the stomach, and then contracts to prevent stomach acids from backing up into the esophagus.” ([23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-3-the-mouth-pharynx-and-esophagus), CC BY 4.0)
9. A tissue called stratified squamous epithelium, made of many layers of cells, lines the esophagus and protects it from wear by food. *(defines “stratified squamous epithelium”)*
   > “The mucosa of the esophagus is made up of an epithelial lining that contains non-keratinized, stratified squamous epithelium, with a layer of basal and parabasal cells. This epithelium protects against erosion from food particles.” ([23.3 The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/23-3-the-mouth-pharynx-and-esophagus), CC BY 4.0)
   > “stratified squamous epithelium: tissue that consists of multiple layers of cells with the most apical being flat scale-like cells; protects surfaces from abrasion” ([Chapter 4 Key Terms (The Tissue Level of Organization)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)
10. Glands in the inner lining release mucus, a thick, slippery substance that keeps the lining moist and helps food pass. *(defines “mucus”)*
   > “The mucosa has glands that secrete mucus to keep the lining moist and well lubricated to ease the passage of food.” ([SEER Training Modules: Pharynx & Esophagus](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/regions/pharynx.html), Free of copyright (NCI reuse policy))
   > “mucous gland: group of cells that secrete mucous, a thick, slippery substance that keeps tissues moist and acts as a lubricant” ([Chapter 4 Key Terms (The Tissue Level of Organization)](https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/4-key-terms), CC BY 4.0)

#### Gallbladder: Plain (drafted; grade 8.6; `content/FMA_7202/tier1.md`)

1. The gallbladder stores, concentrates, and releases bile, a digestive juice made by the liver. *(defines “bile”)*
